assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED turned a superconducting circuit into a controllable artificial atom strongly coupled to a single microwave photon, opening a clean new regime of light-matter interaction (strong coupling, dispersive readout, vacuum Rabi splitting on a chip). It is the enabling platform for superconducting qubits, microwave quantum optics and waveguide QED, and the field has since been robust across many laboratories. The discovery, not the application, is what is rewarded, and here the physics is basic and general.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the first strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff et al., Schoelkopf group) are the decisive pair. Schoelkopf and Wallraff carry the experimental realization, Girvin the theory leadership; Blais is a close fourth and the three-name limit forces a hard choice. I am close to this community, so I weigh the allocation cautiously and acknowledge possible bias.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: two decades of independent confirmation, widely reproduced across groups and platforms, and a stable interpretation. The 2025 prize recognized macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which is a related but distinct discovery, so recognition of cQED is timely rather than premature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits may make the committee hesitant to reward the same platform so soon.
Allocation among Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff is genuinely contested and I cannot verify exact historical credit independently.
My own proximity to the field and to WACQT is a potential conflict of interest.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions defined a physically concrete architecture for quantum computation, and ion experiments realized high-fidelity gates, entanglement of many ions and small algorithms. The work made quantum information processing an experimental discipline and remains a benchmark platform. It is a clear case of foundational physics turning into an enabling platform.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the decisive 1995 theory contribution. Blatt led much of the European experimental realization (gates, multi-ion entanglement, quantum simulation); Wineland, already a laureate, is not on the list. The trio is plausible, though other experimentalists (for example Monroe) are not credited and this affects fairness.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with strong confirmation across multiple independent ion groups and steady fidelity improvements. Recognition is timely, as 2012 recognized ion control for metrology and this concerns the computing proposal.
uncertainties: The credited names omit key experimentalists such as Monroe, so the experimental credit may be incomplete.
Overlap with the other Cirac and Zoller candidates means the committee must choose how to split theory credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault-tolerant ideas show that errors can be suppressed in principle, which is the conceptual foundation for any large quantum computer. Surface-code and topological ideas have also shaped condensed matter and device design. I stress, as a practitioner, that we will not know how to use quantum processors until error correction is realized at scale.
assessment.attribution: Shor (nine-qubit code, fault tolerance), Steane (CSS-type codes) and Kitaev (toric code, topological fault tolerance) are plausible core contributors, but others such as Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme and Preskill contributed centrally. Credit is spread, so a three-person prize looks fragile.
assessment.maturity: Theoretically settled, and experiments are now showing below-threshold logical error suppression on superconducting and atomic platforms. Experimental demonstration is still early, so I consider it somewhat premature as a physics discovery.
uncertainties: Diffuse credit among many theorists makes a fair three-person allocation hard.
Whether this is a discovery in physics or mathematics and computer science is debatable.
Large-scale fault tolerance has not been demonstrated yet.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics and quantum acoustics brought massive mechanical oscillators into the quantum regime: ground-state cooling, sideband cooling, squeezing and entanglement of mechanical motion, and quantum control of phonons coupled to superconducting qubits. This opens a new regime relevant to quantum transduction and tests of quantum mechanics at larger mass scales. It is close to my own work on propagating phonons coupled to artificial atoms.
assessment.attribution: Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer are central to cavity optomechanics, and Cleland to quantum acoustics and the first quantum ground state of a mechanical resonator. Others (O'Connell et al., Painter, Lehnert, Teufel, Schwab) also contributed and the field is a compound of optical and electrical approaches, so credit is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Experiments have been reproduced by multiple laboratories and the interpretation is stable, but applications such as transduction are not yet established. Recognition would be reasonable though the field is still developing.
uncertainties: Compound discovery with several parallel experimental platforms; omitted contributors may have equal claim.
Whether the subfield has yet produced a single clean, decisive discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength idea, achieve fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and make precision tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy possible. This is a clean experiment where every systematic is understood in physical detail.
assessment.attribution: Katori's proposal and first realization are decisive; Ye's group pushed the accuracy and precision record. Two laureates is a natural, compact configuration, though other groups (Lemonde, Gill, Hinkley/Ludlow) contributed. Ye also appears under ultracold molecules.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent confirmation from many national metrology laboratories, and a redefinition of the second is under discussion. Timely, though 2005 and 2012 prizes already covered the frequency comb and ion clocks.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier prizes in precision measurement may lower priority.
Credit beyond the two names could be argued.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution was an early demonstration that quantum mechanics changes the rules of information processing, with BB84 and the entanglement-based E91 protocol connecting to Bell tests. Its conceptual originality is high, and it has been implemented over long distances and from satellites.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) are clear; Ekert's E91 is a distinct, independent route, and Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea complicates priority. The credited trio is reasonable but not free of dispute.
assessment.maturity: Protocols are well established and field-tested, but practical security relies on implementation details, and whether the topic is physics or applied cryptography is debated. Timing is plausible, particularly after the 2022 Bell-test prize.
uncertainties: Priority dispute with Wiesner, who died in 2021 and cannot be recognised.
The 2022 prize already covered entanglement and Bell tests, so overlap is possible.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade enables programmable neutral-atom arrays with tweezers for quantum simulation and computing, including quantum phase transitions and recent logical-qubit demonstrations. A fast-moving platform with real new physics in controlled many-body dynamics.
assessment.attribution: Lukin, Browaeys and Saffman each made central experimental or theoretical contributions; Zoller proposed the gate and is on the list in other candidates. Dropping him is a visible credit gap.
assessment.maturity: Rapid progress but the field is still maturing, and the platform's long-term standing relative to superconducting and ion systems is not settled. Probably premature for now.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond established a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a versatile nanoscale sensor, with wide use in physics, chemistry and biology. The discovery is clear and has been very widely reproduced.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko made the first single-center optical detection and control; Lukin contributed to coherent control and sensing proposals, though his contribution is more spread, and Gruber et al. also made the 1997 single-NV observation.
assessment.maturity: Mature and reproducible across hundreds of laboratories, with a strong sensing application base. Timing is reasonable, but some recognition may focus on applications.
uncertainties: Lukin's credit is broad and less specific to the original discovery.
Application value may outweigh a single foundational discovery.
